name: Linear Regression
short_description: Models a continuous outcome as a linear combination of input features using Ordinary Least Squares.
intuition: Fits a straight line (or flat hyperplane in multi-dimensions) through the data points so that the total squared vertical distances from the points to the line are as small as possible.
step_by_step_working: Center or standardize features if needed.
Calculate the weight matrix using the closed-form normal equation: beta = (X^T * X)^(-1) * X^T * y.
Predict target values: y_hat = X * beta.
Compute residuals and calculate evaluation metrics (MAE, RMSE, R²).

parameters.name: fit_intercept
parameters.description: Whether to calculate the intercept for this model. If set to False, no intercept will be used in calculations.

advantages: Highly interpretable with intuitive, explainable coefficients.
Fastest training and inference speed of any regression model.
limitations: Assumes strict linearity between features and target.
Vulnerable to severe distortion from outliers and multicollinear features.
use_cases: Predicting real estate sales prices from square footage and bedrooms.
Estimating future revenue growth based on marketing expenditure.
when_to_use: When a fast, transparent baseline is needed.
When relationships between features and target are approximately linear.
when_to_avoid: When non-linear relationships and complex interactions dominate the data.
python_snippet:
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
model = LinearRegression(fit_intercept=True)
model.fit(X_train, y_train)
y_pred = model.predict(X_test)
code_explanation: Instantiates and fits Ordinary Least Squares linear regression. Coefficients can be inspected with model.coef_ and intercept with model.intercept_.

name: Ridge Regression
short_description: Linear regression with L2 Tikhonov regularization penalty to mitigate multicollinearity and overfitting.
intuition: Like linear regression, but pulls all coefficient sizes smoothly toward zero. It prevents any single feature from having a wildly disproportionate influence.
step_by_step_working: Standardize all feature columns.
Add L2 penalty matrix alpha * I to X^T * X.
Solve regularized normal equation: beta = (X^T * X + alpha * I)^(-1) * X^T * y.
Generate predictions on standardized test features.

parameters.name: alpha
parameters.description: Regularization strength; must be a positive float. Larger values specify stronger regularization.

advantages: Stable even when features are highly correlated (multicollinearity).
Guarantees an invertible matrix solution even when p > n.
limitations: Retains all features; does not perform sparse feature selection.
Features must be scaled before fitting.
use_cases: Economic forecasting with hundreds of correlated economic indicators.
Sensor telemetry regression where sensors measure overlapping physical properties.
when_to_use: When linear regression overfits due to multicollinear features.
When you want to keep all features in the model with restrained weights.
when_to_avoid: When you need a sparse model with automatic feature selection (use Lasso instead).
python_snippet:
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge
model = Ridge(alpha=1.0)
model.fit(X_train_scaled, y_train)
y_pred = model.predict(X_test_scaled)
code_explanation: Ridge fits regularized weights with alpha=1.0. Features must be standardized so the L2 penalty affects all coefficients equally.

name: Lasso Regression
short_description: Linear regression with L1 regularization penalty that drives redundant feature coefficients to exactly zero.
intuition: Lasso penalizes the absolute sum of weights. Its geometric diamond constraint forces unneeded feature weights to hit zero, leaving you with a simplified model using only the essential features.
step_by_step_working: Standardize all feature inputs.
Optimize coefficients using coordinate descent with L1 soft-thresholding.
Identify features whose weights shrink to exactly 0.0.
Predict continuous outcomes using the remaining sparse features.

parameters.name: alpha
parameters.description: Constant that multiplies the L1 term. Defaults to 0.1.

advantages: Performs automatic feature selection, producing sparse and highly explainable models.
limitations: If a group of features are highly correlated, Lasso arbitrarily selects just one.
use_cases: Gene expression analysis with thousands of candidate genes and few samples.
Click-through rate prediction with high-dimensional sparse bag-of-words features.
when_to_use: When you have many features and suspect only a few are truly predictive.
When a compact, sparse model is required for fast production inference.
when_to_avoid: When all features have genuine predictive value and none should be discarded.
python_snippet:
from sklearn.linear_model import Lasso
model = Lasso(alpha=0.1)
model.fit(X_train_scaled, y_train)
y_pred = model.predict(X_test_scaled)
code_explanation: Fits L1-regularized regression. Inspecting model.coef_ == 0 shows which features were safely eliminated by Lasso.

name: Decision Tree Regressor
short_description: Non-linear regression that recursively partitions feature space into rectangles, predicting the mean target in each leaf.
intuition: Creates an inverted tree of simple questions (e.g., 'Is age > 40?'). When a query reaches a terminal leaf node, the model predicts the average target value of all training points that landed in that leaf.
step_by_step_working: Evaluate all candidate feature thresholds to find the split minimizing child mean squared error.
Split samples into left and right subsets.
Repeat recursively until stopping conditions (max_depth, min_samples_leaf) are reached.
Assign the average target value of the leaf as the prediction for any sample falling in it.

parameters.name: max_depth
parameters.description: The maximum depth of the tree. Controls model complexity and prevents overfitting.

parameters.name: min_samples_split
parameters.description: The minimum number of samples required to split an internal node.

advantages: Captures complex non-linear relationships without feature transformations.
Completely invariant to monotonic feature scaling.
limitations: Prone to heavy overfitting if allowed to grow deep without pruning.
Predicts step-wise constant values; cannot extrapolate beyond the min/max values seen in training.
use_cases: Predicting manufacturing cycle times where distinct equipment thresholds trigger delays.
Estimating insurance claims based on rule-like driver risk segments.
when_to_use: When relationships are non-linear or threshold-driven.
When you need a fast, interpretable tree structure.
when_to_avoid: When continuous smooth extrapolation is required.
When high accuracy without tree-pruning tuning is desired.
python_snippet:
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor
model = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=5, random_state=42)
model.fit(X_train, y_train)
y_pred = model.predict(X_test)
code_explanation: Fits a decision tree regressor capped at depth 5 to avoid overfitting.

name: Random Forest Regressor
short_description: An ensemble of de-correlated decision trees trained on bootstrap samples that averages predictions to slash variance.
intuition: Instead of relying on a single tree that might overfit, build a forest of 100 diverse trees on random slices of data and features. Average their individual predictions to produce a smooth, stable, and accurate forecast.
step_by_step_working: Generate B bootstrap samples of the training data (sampling with replacement).
For each sample, grow a regression tree, randomly selecting a subset of features at each split.
Grow trees deep without pruning.
For a new test point, pass it down every tree in the forest and compute the average predicted value.

parameters.name: n_estimators
parameters.description: The number of trees in the forest.

parameters.name: max_depth
parameters.description: Maximum depth of each decision tree in the ensemble.

advantages: Exceptional out-of-the-box accuracy on tabular data.
Highly resistant to overfitting compared to individual decision trees.
limitations: Slower to train and requires more memory than linear models.
Cannot extrapolate trends beyond the training target range.
use_cases: Predicting patient length of hospital stay.
Forecasting energy consumption in smart buildings.
when_to_use: When non-linear interactions are present and top predictive performance is the priority.
When tabular data has mixed categorical and continuous columns.
when_to_avoid: When ultra-fast sub-millisecond inference on low-power devices is required.
When a single explainable linear formula is legally mandatory.
python_snippet:
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor
model = RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=100, max_depth=10, random_state=42)
model.fit(X_train, y_train)
y_pred = model.predict(X_test)
code_explanation: Trains an ensemble of 100 regression trees in parallel. The .predict() method averages outputs across all trees.

name: Gradient Boosting Regressor
short_description: Sequentially builds an ensemble of shallow trees, where each new tree is trained to correct the residual errors of the previous ones.
intuition: Unlike Random Forests which build trees in parallel, Gradient Boosting builds trees in a relay team. Tree 1 makes a rough prediction. Tree 2 specifically studies where Tree 1 made mistakes (the residuals) and predicts those mistakes. Tree 3 corrects the remaining errors, gradually refining accuracy.
step_by_step_working: Initialize model with a constant prediction (mean of y).
For each boosting iteration: compute pseudo-residuals (negative gradient of loss).
Fit a shallow regression tree h_m(x) to predict the pseudo-residuals.
Scale the tree's output by the learning rate and add it to the running ensemble: F_m(x) = F_(m-1)(x) + lr * h_m(x).
Repeat until n_estimators iterations are completed.

parameters.name: n_estimators
parameters.description: The number of boosting stages to perform.

parameters.name: learning_rate
parameters.description: Learning rate shrinks the contribution of each tree. Must be positive.

parameters.name: max_depth
parameters.description: Maximum depth of individual regression estimators.

advantages: State-of-the-art predictive accuracy on complex tabular benchmarks.
Flexible loss functions (least squares, least absolute deviation, Huber).
Strong modeling of subtle non-linear interactions.
limitations: Sequential training makes it slower than parallel Random Forests.
More hyperparameters to tune; can overfit if learning rate is too high or trees are too deep.
use_cases: Financial risk modeling and algorithmic pricing.
Predicting flight delay durations based on weather and air traffic patterns.
when_to_use: When maximizing predictive accuracy (RMSE / R²) is the top objective.
When dataset has structured numerical features with subtle interdependencies.
when_to_avoid: When training time must be instantaneous.
When data is noisy with severe mislabeled target values.
python_snippet:
from sklearn.ensemble import GradientBoostingRegressor
model = GradientBoostingRegressor(n_estimators=100, learning_rate=0.1, max_depth=3, random_state=42)
model.fit(X_train, y_train)
y_pred = model.predict(X_test)
code_explanation: Trains a gradient boosted ensemble of 100 shallow trees sequentially, each minimizing residual loss with learning_rate=0.1.
